findings.section: The cookie/auth package (binding) + Phase 4
findings.message: The package is internally incoherent on the single path John uses most: clicking buttons. It decrees (a) the cookie authorizes GET rows ONLY, (b) every mutating POST requires the raw header token, and (c) the raw token never reaches the page — enrollment sets an HttpOnly HMAC cookie the JS cannot read, the token never rides a URL, and ANCHOR_BOOT carries 'token presence', not the token. Put together: after a successful /login, the extracted frontend's _postJson has NOTHING to put in X-Anchor-Token, so the moment a mutating route flips to enforce, every dashboard button — done/add/capture, term_start, kill, advance, grass, the entire R&D surface — answers 401 for a fully enrolled browser. The warn-mode soak would even mask this until the flip (warn logs 'would 401' and allows through). The frustrated-UX apex: John logs in correctly and his tool stops working. The package must pick and specify a mechanism — hand the page a mutation credential at login (weakening the XSS story it brags about), or let cookie+custom-header+Origin checks authorize mutations (contradicting 'cookie authorizes GET only'), or something else — and re-derive the CSRF posture from that choice. As written the binding block cannot be implemented without silently deviating from it.

findings.section: Phase 5 / writer model failure mode (b)
findings.message: 'Supervisor down → the inline seam runs the job in-process' is defined as a data/ownership story but has NO user-visible surfacing. Post-5b John's mental model becomes 'restarts don't kill jobs' — the entire point of C4. But if the supervisor service is down (crashed, stopped by an installer, the duplicate-instance guard fired) the dashboard silently degrades to inline, John launches a Foreman build believing it is restart-safe, restarts the dashboard mid-wave, and the job dies in exactly the pre-split way — with the plan's own drain-script quiescence check now downgraded to 'informational', so nothing even blocks him. The hybrid-state matrix names the configuration for the healthcheck, but the DASHBOARD must loudly show which mode a launch will get (banner/badge at launch time), and the drain script's downgrade must be conditional on external mode being live, not on Phase 5b having shipped. Otherwise C4's guarantee is true only sometimes, unpredictably, which is worse UX than never.

findings.section: Phase 0 drain script + per-wave smoke ritual
findings.message: The drain script now BLOCKS while a lane job is in flight, and every wave's merge requires the smoke ritual (drain → nssm restart). Lane jobs are trio runs — researchPrime/Crucible/Foreman routinely run for hours, and John's stated workflow keeps them running concurrently with other work (a ship-Anchor-v1 build is literally parked awaiting concurrent execution). So for Phases 0 through 5a — the majority of the plan's waves — every merge either (a) stalls behind job quiescence for hours, wrecking wave cadence, or (b) trains John/Foreman to reach for the --override flag habitually, normalizing exactly the in-flight-work loss the check exists to prevent. The plan sizes this cost at zero. It needs a stated policy: deploy windows negotiated around job schedules, or the smoke ritual explicitly permitted to queue until quiescence, with the wave-cadence impact acknowledged in the phase sizes.

findings.section: Phase 0 drain script ('costs a warm reconnect, not dead context')
findings.message: The plan repeats ~15–20 live-service restarts (one per merged wave) and claims each 'costs a warm reconnect, not dead context.' That is an overclaim: parking a live PTY kills the live engine process; the W3 warm-resume seed is a cached SUMMARY plus doc pointers, not the in-flight conversation state. A mid-task interactive session — half-answered gate questions, un-persisted working context, the model's own attention on the problem — is materially degraded by park+reseed, and the ConPTY-'no' branch leans on this same fallback as 'a paperwork step.' Multiply by every wave over weeks and John's daily interactive work is repeatedly chopped by the very effort promising 'John's daily use never breaks.' The plan should state the real cost honestly (summary-grade resume, not continuity), batch merges to reduce restart count, and make the PTY-survival spike's economic bar reflect that the fallback is lossy, not free.

findings.section: Cookie/auth package + Phase 0 cookie spike
findings.message: The spike's acceptance questions verify cookie TRANSMISSION (profile jar sharing, WS upgrade survival) on both clients, but never cookie PERSISTENCE on the iPhone/iPad PWA. Max-Age 365 is asserted as if the client honors it; iOS/WebKit ITP and standalone-web-app storage eviction are known to purge site data on their own schedule regardless of Max-Age. If the cookie evaporates every N days, the enrollment story becomes: John, on his phone, repeatedly re-pasting a long random token into a login form — the single most friction-laden flow in the whole package, recurring. The spike must add an explicit longevity/eviction acceptance question for the iOS PWA (and a fallback answer if it fails — e.g. re-enroll UX that reads the token from a password manager cleanly), or C2's 'browser page navigation still working' is only demonstrated for day one.

findings.section: Cookie/auth package — enrollment flow
findings.message: Two compounding navigation frustrations are baked in as specified. (1) The enrollment flow is 'GET /x → 302 /login → POST /api/login → redirect /' — the originally requested URL is discarded, so any deep link (a /project/<id> bookmark, a /summary link from a report, a stale tab's 409-driven trip through /login) dumps John on the home dashboard and makes him re-navigate. Preserving the return-to target is table stakes for a login redirect and is unspecified. (2) SameSite=Strict withholds the cookie on cross-site-initiated top-level navigations — clicking a dashboard link from an email, a note, Slack, or another app arrives cookieless, bouncing an ALREADY-ENROLLED John to /login (and then, per (1), to the wrong page). SameSite=Lax on the GET-only cookie preserves the CSRF posture (Lax still withholds on cross-site POST, and mutations require the header anyway) while fixing the bounce; the package chose Strict without weighing this cost. Both need explicit resolution in the binding block.

findings.section: Phase 3 three-class parity gate + Scenarios A/B
findings.message: The gate's UX contradicts its own taxonomy. REPAIRABLE is defined as the EXPECTED artifact of the chosen journal-first ordering, yet it presents identically to catastrophe: parity=RED, dashboard banner, healthcheck report demanding John run a two-step CLI (--dry-run then --apply). Worse, Scenario A's tail-window footnote creates REPAIRABLE REDs that require NOTHING (they self-heal next run) — so the same RED banner sometimes means 'do nothing', sometimes 'run the tool', and (as BUG) 'stop and root-cause'. A single-user dashboard whose red banner has historically meant 'healthcheck failed' cannot afford a cry-wolf RED for by-design states; John will learn to ignore it, which is how the one real BUG gets ignored too. Meanwhile growing-repairable — new orphaned intents appearing run over run, i.e. a systemic emit-then-crash defect — merely 'escalates a WARN-investigate line while staying REPAIRABLE', soft-pedaling the one repairable pattern that IS alarming. The classes need distinct visual severities (repairable ≠ RED), the self-healing skew case should never banner at all, and the justification for refusing auto-replay of the by-definition-idempotent-safe class deserves a real cost/benefit rather than a decree — the current design converts an 'expected artifact' into recurring manual chores plus alarm fatigue.

findings.section: Phase 0 contract shim / per-wave deploys
findings.message: Every wave's deploy bumps the build id, so every long-lived tab, the desktop app window, and the iPad/iPhone PWA all present a manual 'reload required' banner after each of ~15–20 merges. The mechanism is correct (better than silent breakage) but the plan never considers auto-reloading the idle GET-only case (a page that hasn't posted anything can location.reload() itself safely), so the shim converts each deploy into a small tax collected on every open surface John owns, for weeks. Specify auto-reload-when-idle or accept the tax explicitly.

findings.section: Cookie/auth package — /api/login + lockout runbook
findings.message: POST /api/login is 'rate-limited to blunt token guessing', but the lockout-recovery runbook only covers token LOSS (nssm get / token show / unset+restart). The mundane case — John fat-fingers the long random token three times on a phone keyboard and trips his own rate limiter on his own LAN — has no specified limit parameters, no reset path short of a service restart, and no statement of whether the limiter keys per-IP (Tailscale proxy may collapse all clients to one source IP, so one bad device could lock out all of them). Specify the limiter's shape and its recovery, or it will be discovered live.

findings.section: Cookie/auth package — token-unset behavior + Phase 4 ops-cutover
findings.message: Token-unset yields 'a standing dashboard banner' stating the service runs unauthenticated. Phase 4 explicitly contemplates John DECLINING tokened ops (recorded as an amendment) — in which case his accepted, deliberate, localhost-only configuration nags him with a permanent banner in the tool he looks at every day, forever. A recorded amendment should be able to acknowledge the state (dismissible banner, or a one-line footer chip) rather than treating the owner's documented decision as a perpetual warning condition.

findings.section: Walked Scenario A / rnd events CLI
findings.message: Scenario A explicitly lets job_launched sort before job_launch_requested in the browse order and calls it acceptable because browse order is presentational — but the browse order's primary consumer is a human debugging dual-write via `rnd events`, and a causally inverted timeline is exactly the kind of output that makes an operator distrust the journal. Since every effect event carries a causation edge, the merge could offer a --causal ordering (topo-sort within correlation groups) at near-zero cost; worth a line in Phase 3.

findings.section: Writer model failure mode (b) + Phase 5b drain-check downgrade
findings.message: Two of the plan's own provisions compose to recreate exactly the loss class C4 forbids. Failure mode (b) says supervisor-down -> the inline seam runs the job in-process (mode:'inline'), and Phase 5b simultaneously downgrades the drain script's lane-job quiescence check to informational 'because jobs now survive a dashboard restart by construction.' They do NOT survive in degraded mode: supervisor service dies -> next launch silently runs inline inside the dashboard -> a routine wave deploy runs the drain (now informational, does not block) -> nssm restart anchor kills the in-flight inline job. Nothing in the plan requires degraded/inline mode to be loudly surfaced to the operator — no dashboard banner, no healthcheck assertion that flag=external implies a LIVE supervisor (Phase 6 asserts the flag configuration, not the runtime liveness behind it). John believes restart-survival holds precisely when it doesn't. Required: (i) a mandatory operator-visible degraded-mode signal (banner + healthcheck liveness assert, not just an envelope field), and (ii) the quiescence-check downgrade must be conditional per-job on the job actually being supervisor-owned (check the job's mode), never unconditional on 'Phase 5b shipped.'

findings.section: Cookie/auth package — lockout recovery & rotation; Phase 5b IPC auth
findings.message: The rotation runbook ('set a new token + restart') was written for one service, but Phase 5b makes ANCHOR_TOKEN the shared secret for dashboard<->supervisor IPC, stored in TWO services' AppEnvironmentExtra. Rotation now requires updating and restarting BOTH services; in the mismatch window the dashboard cannot launch, cancel, tail, or gate-answer jobs — operator-visible breakage of the exact IPC rows the contract table hardens, potentially with a job in flight. No rotation choreography, restart ordering, or defined mismatch behavior appears anywhere; the lockout runbook names only the anchor service. The cookie package's 'no state exists in which John is locked out' claim is unproven for the two-service world it will actually run in.

findings.section: Phase 5b IPC auth / per-wave smoke ritual
findings.message: The plan builds an entire versioning shim (X-Anchor-Build, 409, pre-auth ordering) for frontend<->backend skew, then creates a second, worse skew surface and says nothing about it: journal.py, the route-table module, and the IPC contract are SHARED code across two independently restartable NSSM services, each of which picks up a wave's deploy only at its own restart. Post-5b the smoke ritual still restarts only `anchor`, so the supervisor can run last week's envelope schema or contract semantics indefinitely — and a shared-module wave that DOES need a supervisor restart has no stated deploy order or in-flight-job handling. Required: an IPC contract-version handshake (mismatch -> defined degrade, not undefined behavior) and a deploy-order rule in the post-5b smoke ritual.

findings.section: Three-class parity gate; Scenario B
findings.message: The gate reports the SAME top-level RED for the expected, benign, self-inflicted artifact of journal-first ordering (REPAIRABLE) and for never-should-happen corruption (BUG); the operator must read the census rows to know which. On a one-operator system this is textbook alarm-fatigue design — Scenario B itself normalizes a WEEK of RED with 'the operator did nothing,' which is exactly how the existing red health banner gets trained into invisibility, so the day a real legacy-ahead BUG lands it reads as 'that repairable thing again.' REPAIRABLE should be a distinct amber/WARN top-level state with its named rows and replay call-to-action; RED reserved exclusively for BUG. The state machine already distinguishes them internally — the operator signal should too.

findings.section: Phase 5b probes (a)-(c); Phase 6 healthcheck wiring
findings.message: Probe (b) restarts the LIVE supervisor with a sacrificial child to prove breakaway, and Phase 6 wires 'supervisor probes' into the 5AM run without distinguishing one-time acceptance probes from recurring daily walks. As written, the plan restarts a production service every morning at 5AM — precisely when John's overnight trio jobs are most likely in flight — betting on job-object breakaway and job re-adoption working every single night, forever, as a TEST. Probes (a) and (c) are cheap and recurring-safe; (b) must be explicitly classified as an acceptance/runbook probe (run at 5b sign-off and after supervisor-touching deploys), not a daily ritual. The plan currently doesn't say, and the default reading is operator-hostile.

findings.section: Phase 0 drain script; per-wave smoke ritual
findings.message: Every merged wave of Phases 1-4 (~12+ waves) ends in drain -> nssm restart, and the drain BLOCKS while any lane job is in flight. John's real lane jobs are Foreman builds and research runs that hold for hours, often overnight, often on OTHER projects than this one. The plan prices this collision at a single override flag that 'logs the acceptance of loss' — i.e., the sanctioned path is either stalling the re-architecture behind unrelated project work for hours per wave, or normalizing killing other projects' in-flight jobs. A months-long effort needs a stated wave-deploy scheduling policy (deploy windows, coordination with the job calendar, or batching multiple waves per restart) — not a per-incident moral choice at the drain prompt.

findings.section: DAG re-cut; Phase 5a scheduling claim
findings.message: The re-cut's headline — 'the jobs-half now starts at the plan's midpoint (5a concurrent with 4)' — cannot be realized by the execution engine this plan hands off to: Foreman runs single-threaded, one wave at a time (the standing trio coding rule), so 5a and 4 will serialize in practice, and genuinely interleaving their waves would hold two phases' half-done state in one working tree on shared modules (the route-table module is Phase 4 wave 1 AND 5b's dependency). The Round-2 press is answered on paper only. Either state the actual serialized wave order (in which case say honestly where the jobs-half really starts) or specify concretely how Foreman interleaves two phases' waves without cross-contamination.

findings.section: Scenario A tail-window footnote vs Scenario B non-flapping claim
findings.message: Scenario A's footnote admits an NTP step-back can transiently classify a healthy in-flight event REPAIRABLE (RED) that self-clears on the next run; Scenario B claims reports are 'unchanged, not flapping.' A 5AM RED that has vanished by the time the operator reruns on demand IS a flap, and it burns operator trust for nothing. Require a repairable row to persist across two consecutive runs before the top-level signal degrades, or key the window on per-writer seq distance rather than wall ts alone.

findings.section: Tier-2 parity gate window sizing
findings.message: The 60s window is sized 'an order of magnitude above plausible NTP steps' — but the relevant race isn't clocks, it's legacy-write latency: the doc-persisted legacy write is a git add/commit (persist_session_docs), which on a large worktree or under lock contention can plausibly exceed 60s. A Tier-2 snapshot landing in that gap classifies a healthy in-flight dual-write REPAIRABLE/RED. Size the window against measured worst-case legacy-write latency per event type (the doc-persist family may need its own larger window), not against NTP alone.

findings.section: Phase 0 cookie spike acceptance questions; cookie/auth package
findings.message: The spike's pre-written acceptance questions cover cookie-jar sharing and WS-upgrade survival but NOT persistence: iOS/WebKit storage eviction on home-screen PWAs can evict cookies after ~7 days of disuse regardless of Max-Age=365d, which for John means periodic token re-entry on the iPad — an operator annoyance the package's 'zero breaks' enrollment story doesn't account for. Add persistence-across-days / across-relaunch / across-reboot to the spike's acceptance questions with a stated fallback if it fails.

findings.section: healthcheck_repeat.py; Phase 6 walk wiring
findings.message: Letting all 20 consecutive greens run back-to-back in one accelerated session samples one process, one quiescence state, one uptime, one time-of-day — precisely NOT the 5AM environment the requirement exists to protect (the historical flakes were environmental: port squatting, quiescence, service-account state). Require a minimum quota of real scheduled-run greens (e.g., 5 nightly among the 20) before any walk joins the 5AM run; accelerated runs may fill the remainder.

findings.section: Phase 5b install_supervisor.ps1
findings.message: install_supervisor.ps1 specifies ObjectName, env cloning, and CREATE_NO_WINDOW, but child survival across a supervisor restart also depends on NSSM's stop behavior (kill-process-tree / stop-method settings) and the breakaway job-object config — none stated. Probe (b) would catch a miss, but only at live-deploy time; put the stop-behavior settings in the script spec so the first live run isn't the discovery mechanism.

findings.section: Phase 2 migration vs Phase 6 scaffolding retirement
findings.message: Phase 2 preserves the old data dir 'read-only for a week,' but Phase 6 — several L-sized phases later — 'concludes the old data dir's read-only week and archives it.' Both cannot be literal. Say which is meant: retention for one calendar week after the migration, or retention until closure (the safer reading, but then stop calling it a week).

findings.section: Shim pre-list ordering (Phase 0 / cookie package / Phase 4 front door)
findings.message: Ordering the X-Anchor-Build check BEFORE auth means any unauthenticated client can harvest the current build id from the structured 409's `expected` field. The UX rationale is sound and the leak is trivial, but a plan this rigorous about OPEN_ROUTES justifications should record the pre-auth 409 as an accepted, reviewed disclosure (one line in the OPEN_ROUTES artifact or the package), not leave it implicit.

findings.section: Phase 3 — two-tier parity gate / writer model
findings.message: The Tier-2 gate 'derives views from a WRITE_LOCK-bracketed snapshot copy' — but WRITE_LOCK is an in-process lock in the DASHBOARD. Post-split, the supervisor appends to its own segment and writes its own legacy job records concurrently, outside any lock the snapshot can take. If the snapshot copies the journal segments BEFORE the legacy stores, a supervisor write landing between the two copies produces a legacy-ahead delta — which your own classification calls BUG, never-self-clearing, phase-gate-blocking. The plan never specifies snapshot ordering (legacy-first, journal-second, so the journal is always at-least-as-new) nor acknowledges that the lock cannot bracket a second process. As written, the live gate can manufacture false BUGs on a healthy post-split system, and BUG is defined as un-clearable. Specify the cross-store snapshot ordering as binding, and re-walk Scenario A/B against the two-process case.

findings.section: Phase 3 — emit() fail-open rule + three-class parity gate
findings.message: The fail-open rule makes emit() failure a DESIGNED-TOLERATED event ('logs loudly, counter increments, legacy write proceeds'), and the plan itself says the resulting hole 'shows up as legacy-ahead=BUG'. But BUG is defined as 'never self-clears, blocks the phase gate until root-caused' — and root-causing does not converge the stores. The replay tool only applies journal→legacy; there is no journal-backfill-from-legacy tool, and the 'no writes to journal/ outside journal.py' scan forbids ad-hoc injection. So a single transient disk hiccup during emit produces a permanent, unrepairable RED that blocks gates forever. A tolerated failure mode mapping to an unrepairable gate state is an internal contradiction. Either define a blessed backfill path inside journal.py (emitting a marked reconstruction event), or define a documented BUG-resolution procedure that actually has an edge back to GREEN.

findings.section: Writer model / Scenario B / Phase 3 replay tool
findings.message: Scenario B asserts the replay 'idempotently re-executes the lost legacy write (the pointer-record is written)' — but doc_persisted's legacy effect is not one write; it is copy-files-from-worktree + git commit + pointer-record + index entry. The plan never specifies WHERE in that multi-step sequence emit() sits (journal-first relative to which step?), and if the crash lands before the file copy, the doc bytes exist only in a worktree the boot reaper may since have deleted — the intent is then physically unreplayable from the event, no matter how complete the payload. The payload-completeness gate proves the RECORD is reconstructible, not the EFFECT. The replay tool needs a per-type replayability column (fully-replayable / record-only / unreplayable-report-honestly), and multi-step legacy mutations need a defined emit placement. The walked scenario chose the hardest family and hand-waved exactly its hard part.

findings.section: Phase 5b — live probe (b)
findings.message: Probe (b) asserts a sacrificial child SURVIVES a supervisor restart ('job-object breakaway proven'). But the existing job-object attach (proc_probe.attach_to_job_object, cited by the intake as an asset) exists precisely for owner-dies→children-die orphan prevention, i.e. kill-on-close semantics — under which probe (b) fails BY CONSTRUCTION. Making children survive supervisor restart requires breakaway or dropping KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, which directly weakens the tree-kill cancel path and the zombie/orphan discipline the 2026-06-30 swarm-safety work depends on. The plan asserts the probe as a testable given without naming this design decision (per-job job objects without kill-on-close? explicit tree-kill for cancel + zombie-hunter for orphans?). Note C4 only requires jobs to survive DASHBOARD restart — if supervisor-restart survival is extra hardening, say so and make its job-object configuration an explicit Phase-5a contract row, not an assumed assert.

findings.section: Phase 1 — pinned-fixture dual render
findings.message: The parity gate claims 'diffed byte-for-byte' across all three increments, with an enumerated-delta list for dynamic values. But increment 3's whole point is replacing every server-side {expr} with a window.ANCHOR_BOOT read — a STRUCTURAL delta at every interpolation site. Either the gate defines a normalization step (substitute the boot JSON values into the new static output before diffing, restoring true byte equality), or the enumerated-delta list must whitelist a delta at each of the N interpolation sites — at which point the gate is weakest exactly where the risk concentrates (the census's own 'only genuinely fiddly part'). As written the mechanism is underspecified for the one increment that needs it most; increments 1–2 get a real guarantee, increment 3 gets a list of exemptions. Specify the substitution-normalized diff as the binding mechanism.

findings.section: Scenario A vs Scenario B / C3 state machine
findings.message: Scenario A's tail-window footnote says a clock-step demotion to REPAIRABLE 'self-heals on the next run' once the in-flight legacy write lands. But the binding state machine is stated as exactly 'GREEN → RED(repairable, rows named) → replay --apply → GREEN', and Scenario B's day-7 walk shows REPAIRABLE persisting until an operator acts. Both behaviors are individually sensible (a repairable row whose legacy write subsequently lands stops diverging), but the state machine as written omits the self-clear edge Scenario A relies on — the two walked scenarios contradict the machine that claims to be 'code, not decree'. Add the RED(repairable)→GREEN-without-replay edge (divergence vanished on re-derive) explicitly.

findings.section: Writer model — cli segment
findings.message: Two concurrent anchor.py invocations both recover writer_seq 'from the segment tail'. If the msvcrt/fcntl lock brackets only the APPEND, both read tail=N, both allocate N+1, and the serialized appends produce a duplicate (cli, N+1) — which your gate classifies BUG, never-self-clearing. The lock must bracket read-tail + allocate-seq + append as one critical section; the plan says 'per-append OS file lock', which reads as append-only. One sentence fixes it; unfixed, ordinary concurrent CLI use manufactures permanent BUGs.

findings.section: Phase 4 — wave ordering
findings.message: The cookie/auth package (/login, /api/login, enrollment) and the GET-data-plane enforce flips both live inside Phase 4, but no intra-phase edge orders them: flipping any browser-navigated GET route to enforce before /login ships strands every browser at a 401 (the X-Anchor-Build pre-check only helps stale-BUILD clients, not unenrolled current ones). The plan is explicit about cross-deploy sequencing ('auth flips never ship in the same deploy as the JS calling them') yet silent on this larger ordering. State it as a wave-order rule: enrollment routes + login flow land and soak before the first page-route enforce flip.

findings.section: Cookie/auth package
findings.message: HMAC(fixed-context, ANCHOR_TOKEN) is a DETERMINISTIC value — identical for every client, every device, for the full Max-Age 365d, revocable only by rotating the token itself (which logs out everything). Anyone who observes the cookie once (plain-HTTP localhost sniff, a shared HAR, a synced browser profile) holds a year-long GET credential to the entire data plane including /artifact, with no per-device revocation and no expiry binding. This may be an acceptable trade for a single-user Tailscale-fronted box, but the plan presents the mechanics without recording it as a considered decision; the North Star's 'cookie or equivalent' deserves one sentence of threat-model acceptance (or a cheap improvement: include a server-side epoch/nonce in the HMAC so cookies can be invalidated without token rotation).

findings.section: Phase 0 drain script / per-wave smoke ritual
findings.message: Pre-5b, the drain script BLOCKS while a lane job runs, and every wave's merge requires drain → nssm restart. Real lane jobs (Foreman builds) run for hours and are exactly what John runs daily — so through Phases 0–5a (most of the plan) the deploy cadence is hostage to job quiescence, with the only relief an override that accepts killing the job. The plan states the check but no scheduling mitigation (deploy windows, coordinate with the parked ship-v1 build, queue deploys behind job completion). Name the operational policy now; otherwise C7's 'never-broken increments' quietly becomes 'increments whenever no job is running', discovered mid-build.

findings.section: Dependency DAG — Phase 5a concurrent with Phase 4
findings.message: Under Foreman's single-threaded wave execution, '5a runs CONCURRENT with Phase 4' cannot mean parallel wall-clock work — it means the waves may interleave. The claim 'the jobs-half now starts at the plan's midpoint' is honest as an ordering statement but the DAG's language implies schedule compression that the build topology cannot deliver (except via the warn-soak days, which are calendar waits Phase 5a waves could genuinely fill). Say 'interleavable' and note the soak-day overlap as the actual win.

findings.topic: browser mutation auth undefined after cookie enrollment
findings.section: The cookie/auth package (binding) + Phase 4
findings.message: The package is internally incoherent on the single path John uses most: clicking buttons. It decrees (a) the cookie authorizes GET rows ONLY, (b) every mutating POST requires the raw header token, and (c) the raw token never reaches the page — enrollment sets an HttpOnly HMAC cookie the JS cannot read, the token never rides a URL, and ANCHOR_BOOT carries 'token presence', not the token. Put together: after a successful /login, the extracted frontend's _postJson has NOTHING to put in X-Anchor-Token, so the moment a mutating route flips to enforce, every dashboard button — done/add/capture, term_start, kill, advance, grass, the entire R&D surface — answers 401 for a fully enrolled browser. The warn-mode soak would even mask this until the flip (warn logs 'would 401' and allows through). The frustrated-UX apex: John logs in correctly and his tool stops working. The package must pick and specify a mechanism — hand the page a mutation credential at login (weakening the XSS story it brags about), or let cookie+custom-header+Origin checks authorize mutations (contradicting 'cookie authorizes GET only'), or something else — and re-derive the CSRF posture from that choice. As written the binding block cannot be implemented without silently deviating from it.

findings.topic: silent inline fallback breaks restart-survival predictability
findings.section: Phase 5 / writer model failure mode (b)
findings.message: 'Supervisor down → the inline seam runs the job in-process' is defined as a data/ownership story but has NO user-visible surfacing. Post-5b John's mental model becomes 'restarts don't kill jobs' — the entire point of C4. But if the supervisor service is down (crashed, stopped by an installer, the duplicate-instance guard fired) the dashboard silently degrades to inline, John launches a Foreman build believing it is restart-safe, restarts the dashboard mid-wave, and the job dies in exactly the pre-split way — with the plan's own drain-script quiescence check now downgraded to 'informational', so nothing even blocks him. The hybrid-state matrix names the configuration for the healthcheck, but the DASHBOARD must loudly show which mode a launch will get (banner/badge at launch time), and the drain script's downgrade must be conditional on external mode being live, not on Phase 5b having shipped. Otherwise C4's guarantee is true only sometimes, unpredictably, which is worse UX than never.

findings.topic: pre-5b deploys hostage to hours-long lane jobs
findings.section: Phase 0 drain script + per-wave smoke ritual
findings.message: The drain script now BLOCKS while a lane job is in flight, and every wave's merge requires the smoke ritual (drain → nssm restart). Lane jobs are trio runs — researchPrime/Crucible/Foreman routinely run for hours, and John's stated workflow keeps them running concurrently with other work (a ship-Anchor-v1 build is literally parked awaiting concurrent execution). So for Phases 0 through 5a — the majority of the plan's waves — every merge either (a) stalls behind job quiescence for hours, wrecking wave cadence, or (b) trains John/Foreman to reach for the --override flag habitually, normalizing exactly the in-flight-work loss the check exists to prevent. The plan sizes this cost at zero. It needs a stated policy: deploy windows negotiated around job schedules, or the smoke ritual explicitly permitted to queue until quiescence, with the wave-cadence impact acknowledged in the phase sizes.

findings.topic: warm-resume overclaim across per-wave restarts
findings.section: Phase 0 drain script ('costs a warm reconnect, not dead context')
findings.message: The plan repeats ~15–20 live-service restarts (one per merged wave) and claims each 'costs a warm reconnect, not dead context.' That is an overclaim: parking a live PTY kills the live engine process; the W3 warm-resume seed is a cached SUMMARY plus doc pointers, not the in-flight conversation state. A mid-task interactive session — half-answered gate questions, un-persisted working context, the model's own attention on the problem — is materially degraded by park+reseed, and the ConPTY-'no' branch leans on this same fallback as 'a paperwork step.' Multiply by every wave over weeks and John's daily interactive work is repeatedly chopped by the very effort promising 'John's daily use never breaks.' The plan should state the real cost honestly (summary-grade resume, not continuity), batch merges to reduce restart count, and make the PTY-survival spike's economic bar reflect that the fallback is lossy, not free.

findings.topic: iOS PWA cookie longevity unverified
findings.section: Cookie/auth package + Phase 0 cookie spike
findings.message: The spike's acceptance questions verify cookie TRANSMISSION (profile jar sharing, WS upgrade survival) on both clients, but never cookie PERSISTENCE on the iPhone/iPad PWA. Max-Age 365 is asserted as if the client honors it; iOS/WebKit ITP and standalone-web-app storage eviction are known to purge site data on their own schedule regardless of Max-Age. If the cookie evaporates every N days, the enrollment story becomes: John, on his phone, repeatedly re-pasting a long random token into a login form — the single most friction-laden flow in the whole package, recurring. The spike must add an explicit longevity/eviction acceptance question for the iOS PWA (and a fallback answer if it fails — e.g. re-enroll UX that reads the token from a password manager cleanly), or C2's 'browser page navigation still working' is only demonstrated for day one.

findings.topic: deep-link loss and SameSite=Strict navigation bounce
findings.section: Cookie/auth package — enrollment flow
findings.message: Two compounding navigation frustrations are baked in as specified. (1) The enrollment flow is 'GET /x → 302 /login → POST /api/login → redirect /' — the originally requested URL is discarded, so any deep link (a /project/<id> bookmark, a /summary link from a report, a stale tab's 409-driven trip through /login) dumps John on the home dashboard and makes him re-navigate. Preserving the return-to target is table stakes for a login redirect and is unspecified. (2) SameSite=Strict withholds the cookie on cross-site-initiated top-level navigations — clicking a dashboard link from an email, a note, Slack, or another app arrives cookieless, bouncing an ALREADY-ENROLLED John to /login (and then, per (1), to the wrong page). SameSite=Lax on the GET-only cookie preserves the CSRF posture (Lax still withholds on cross-site POST, and mutations require the header anyway) while fixing the bounce; the package chose Strict without weighing this cost. Both need explicit resolution in the binding block.

findings.topic: REPAIRABLE-RED banner semantics erode operator trust
findings.section: Phase 3 three-class parity gate + Scenarios A/B
findings.message: The gate's UX contradicts its own taxonomy. REPAIRABLE is defined as the EXPECTED artifact of the chosen journal-first ordering, yet it presents identically to catastrophe: parity=RED, dashboard banner, healthcheck report demanding John run a two-step CLI (--dry-run then --apply). Worse, Scenario A's tail-window footnote creates REPAIRABLE REDs that require NOTHING (they self-heal next run) — so the same RED banner sometimes means 'do nothing', sometimes 'run the tool', and (as BUG) 'stop and root-cause'. A single-user dashboard whose red banner has historically meant 'healthcheck failed' cannot afford a cry-wolf RED for by-design states; John will learn to ignore it, which is how the one real BUG gets ignored too. Meanwhile growing-repairable — new orphaned intents appearing run over run, i.e. a systemic emit-then-crash defect — merely 'escalates a WARN-investigate line while staying REPAIRABLE', soft-pedaling the one repairable pattern that IS alarming. The classes need distinct visual severities (repairable ≠ RED), the self-healing skew case should never banner at all, and the justification for refusing auto-replay of the by-definition-idempotent-safe class deserves a real cost/benefit rather than a decree — the current design converts an 'expected artifact' into recurring manual chores plus alarm fatigue.

findings.topic: 409 reload banner on every device every wave
findings.section: Phase 0 contract shim / per-wave deploys
findings.message: Every wave's deploy bumps the build id, so every long-lived tab, the desktop app window, and the iPad/iPhone PWA all present a manual 'reload required' banner after each of ~15–20 merges. The mechanism is correct (better than silent breakage) but the plan never considers auto-reloading the idle GET-only case (a page that hasn't posted anything can location.reload() itself safely), so the shim converts each deploy into a small tax collected on every open surface John owns, for weeks. Specify auto-reload-when-idle or accept the tax explicitly.

findings.topic: login rate-limit lockout has no reset path
findings.section: Cookie/auth package — /api/login + lockout runbook
findings.message: POST /api/login is 'rate-limited to blunt token guessing', but the lockout-recovery runbook only covers token LOSS (nssm get / token show / unset+restart). The mundane case — John fat-fingers the long random token three times on a phone keyboard and trips his own rate limiter on his own LAN — has no specified limit parameters, no reset path short of a service restart, and no statement of whether the limiter keys per-IP (Tailscale proxy may collapse all clients to one source IP, so one bad device could lock out all of them). Specify the limiter's shape and its recovery, or it will be discovered live.

findings.topic: permanent unauthenticated-mode nag banner
findings.section: Cookie/auth package — token-unset behavior + Phase 4 ops-cutover
findings.message: Token-unset yields 'a standing dashboard banner' stating the service runs unauthenticated. Phase 4 explicitly contemplates John DECLINING tokened ops (recorded as an amendment) — in which case his accepted, deliberate, localhost-only configuration nags him with a permanent banner in the tool he looks at every day, forever. A recorded amendment should be able to acknowledge the state (dismissible banner, or a one-line footer chip) rather than treating the owner's documented decision as a perpetual warning condition.

findings.topic: effect-before-intent browse order in the events CLI
findings.section: Walked Scenario A / rnd events CLI
findings.message: Scenario A explicitly lets job_launched sort before job_launch_requested in the browse order and calls it acceptable because browse order is presentational — but the browse order's primary consumer is a human debugging dual-write via `rnd events`, and a causally inverted timeline is exactly the kind of output that makes an operator distrust the journal. Since every effect event carries a causation edge, the merge could offer a --causal ordering (topo-sort within correlation groups) at near-zero cost; worth a line in Phase 3.

findings.topic: silent inline degradation voids C4
findings.section: Writer model failure mode (b) + Phase 5b drain-check downgrade
findings.message: Two of the plan's own provisions compose to recreate exactly the loss class C4 forbids. Failure mode (b) says supervisor-down -> the inline seam runs the job in-process (mode:'inline'), and Phase 5b simultaneously downgrades the drain script's lane-job quiescence check to informational 'because jobs now survive a dashboard restart by construction.' They do NOT survive in degraded mode: supervisor service dies -> next launch silently runs inline inside the dashboard -> a routine wave deploy runs the drain (now informational, does not block) -> nssm restart anchor kills the in-flight inline job. Nothing in the plan requires degraded/inline mode to be loudly surfaced to the operator — no dashboard banner, no healthcheck assertion that flag=external implies a LIVE supervisor (Phase 6 asserts the flag configuration, not the runtime liveness behind it). John believes restart-survival holds precisely when it doesn't. Required: (i) a mandatory operator-visible degraded-mode signal (banner + healthcheck liveness assert, not just an envelope field), and (ii) the quiescence-check downgrade must be conditional per-job on the job actually being supervisor-owned (check the job's mode), never unconditional on 'Phase 5b shipped.'

findings.topic: two-service token rotation atomicity
findings.section: Cookie/auth package — lockout recovery & rotation; Phase 5b IPC auth
findings.message: The rotation runbook ('set a new token + restart') was written for one service, but Phase 5b makes ANCHOR_TOKEN the shared secret for dashboard<->supervisor IPC, stored in TWO services' AppEnvironmentExtra. Rotation now requires updating and restarting BOTH services; in the mismatch window the dashboard cannot launch, cancel, tail, or gate-answer jobs — operator-visible breakage of the exact IPC rows the contract table hardens, potentially with a job in flight. No rotation choreography, restart ordering, or defined mismatch behavior appears anywhere; the lockout runbook names only the anchor service. The cookie package's 'no state exists in which John is locked out' claim is unproven for the two-service world it will actually run in.

findings.topic: dashboard-supervisor version skew
findings.section: Phase 5b IPC auth / per-wave smoke ritual
findings.message: The plan builds an entire versioning shim (X-Anchor-Build, 409, pre-auth ordering) for frontend<->backend skew, then creates a second, worse skew surface and says nothing about it: journal.py, the route-table module, and the IPC contract are SHARED code across two independently restartable NSSM services, each of which picks up a wave's deploy only at its own restart. Post-5b the smoke ritual still restarts only `anchor`, so the supervisor can run last week's envelope schema or contract semantics indefinitely — and a shared-module wave that DOES need a supervisor restart has no stated deploy order or in-flight-job handling. Required: an IPC contract-version handshake (mismatch -> defined degrade, not undefined behavior) and a deploy-order rule in the post-5b smoke ritual.

findings.topic: REPAIRABLE reported as RED
findings.section: Three-class parity gate; Scenario B
findings.message: The gate reports the SAME top-level RED for the expected, benign, self-inflicted artifact of journal-first ordering (REPAIRABLE) and for never-should-happen corruption (BUG); the operator must read the census rows to know which. On a one-operator system this is textbook alarm-fatigue design — Scenario B itself normalizes a WEEK of RED with 'the operator did nothing,' which is exactly how the existing red health banner gets trained into invisibility, so the day a real legacy-ahead BUG lands it reads as 'that repairable thing again.' REPAIRABLE should be a distinct amber/WARN top-level state with its named rows and replay call-to-action; RED reserved exclusively for BUG. The state machine already distinguishes them internally — the operator signal should too.

findings.topic: daily supervisor restart probe
findings.section: Phase 5b probes (a)-(c); Phase 6 healthcheck wiring
findings.message: Probe (b) restarts the LIVE supervisor with a sacrificial child to prove breakaway, and Phase 6 wires 'supervisor probes' into the 5AM run without distinguishing one-time acceptance probes from recurring daily walks. As written, the plan restarts a production service every morning at 5AM — precisely when John's overnight trio jobs are most likely in flight — betting on job-object breakaway and job re-adoption working every single night, forever, as a TEST. Probes (a) and (c) are cheap and recurring-safe; (b) must be explicitly classified as an acceptance/runbook probe (run at 5b sign-off and after supervisor-touching deploys), not a daily ritual. The plan currently doesn't say, and the default reading is operator-hostile.

findings.topic: pre-5b deploy cadence hostage to job quiescence
findings.section: Phase 0 drain script; per-wave smoke ritual
findings.message: Every merged wave of Phases 1-4 (~12+ waves) ends in drain -> nssm restart, and the drain BLOCKS while any lane job is in flight. John's real lane jobs are Foreman builds and research runs that hold for hours, often overnight, often on OTHER projects than this one. The plan prices this collision at a single override flag that 'logs the acceptance of loss' — i.e., the sanctioned path is either stalling the re-architecture behind unrelated project work for hours per wave, or normalizing killing other projects' in-flight jobs. A months-long effort needs a stated wave-deploy scheduling policy (deploy windows, coordination with the job calendar, or batching multiple waves per restart) — not a per-incident moral choice at the drain prompt.

findings.topic: 5a parallel-with-4 is paper parallelism
findings.section: DAG re-cut; Phase 5a scheduling claim
findings.message: The re-cut's headline — 'the jobs-half now starts at the plan's midpoint (5a concurrent with 4)' — cannot be realized by the execution engine this plan hands off to: Foreman runs single-threaded, one wave at a time (the standing trio coding rule), so 5a and 4 will serialize in practice, and genuinely interleaving their waves would hold two phases' half-done state in one working tree on shared modules (the route-table module is Phase 4 wave 1 AND 5b's dependency). The Round-2 press is answered on paper only. Either state the actual serialized wave order (in which case say honestly where the jobs-half really starts) or specify concretely how Foreman interleaves two phases' waves without cross-contamination.

findings.topic: transient REPAIRABLE flap vs stability claim
findings.section: Scenario A tail-window footnote vs Scenario B non-flapping claim
findings.message: Scenario A's footnote admits an NTP step-back can transiently classify a healthy in-flight event REPAIRABLE (RED) that self-clears on the next run; Scenario B claims reports are 'unchanged, not flapping.' A 5AM RED that has vanished by the time the operator reruns on demand IS a flap, and it burns operator trust for nothing. Require a repairable row to persist across two consecutive runs before the top-level signal degrades, or key the window on per-writer seq distance rather than wall ts alone.

findings.topic: tail window vs slow legacy writes
findings.section: Tier-2 parity gate window sizing
findings.message: The 60s window is sized 'an order of magnitude above plausible NTP steps' — but the relevant race isn't clocks, it's legacy-write latency: the doc-persisted legacy write is a git add/commit (persist_session_docs), which on a large worktree or under lock contention can plausibly exceed 60s. A Tier-2 snapshot landing in that gap classifies a healthy in-flight dual-write REPAIRABLE/RED. Size the window against measured worst-case legacy-write latency per event type (the doc-persist family may need its own larger window), not against NTP alone.

findings.topic: iOS PWA cookie longevity absent from spike
findings.section: Phase 0 cookie spike acceptance questions; cookie/auth package
findings.message: The spike's pre-written acceptance questions cover cookie-jar sharing and WS-upgrade survival but NOT persistence: iOS/WebKit storage eviction on home-screen PWAs can evict cookies after ~7 days of disuse regardless of Max-Age=365d, which for John means periodic token re-entry on the iPad — an operator annoyance the package's 'zero breaks' enrollment story doesn't account for. Add persistence-across-days / across-relaunch / across-reboot to the spike's acceptance questions with a stated fallback if it fails.

findings.topic: accelerated 20-greens dilutes the flake gate
findings.section: healthcheck_repeat.py; Phase 6 walk wiring
findings.message: Letting all 20 consecutive greens run back-to-back in one accelerated session samples one process, one quiescence state, one uptime, one time-of-day — precisely NOT the 5AM environment the requirement exists to protect (the historical flakes were environmental: port squatting, quiescence, service-account state). Require a minimum quota of real scheduled-run greens (e.g., 5 nightly among the 20) before any walk joins the 5AM run; accelerated runs may fill the remainder.

findings.topic: NSSM stop-behavior config unstated
findings.section: Phase 5b install_supervisor.ps1
findings.message: install_supervisor.ps1 specifies ObjectName, env cloning, and CREATE_NO_WINDOW, but child survival across a supervisor restart also depends on NSSM's stop behavior (kill-process-tree / stop-method settings) and the breakaway job-object config — none stated. Probe (b) would catch a miss, but only at live-deploy time; put the stop-behavior settings in the script spec so the first live run isn't the discovery mechanism.

findings.topic: read-only-week timeline contradiction
findings.section: Phase 2 migration vs Phase 6 scaffolding retirement
findings.message: Phase 2 preserves the old data dir 'read-only for a week,' but Phase 6 — several L-sized phases later — 'concludes the old data dir's read-only week and archives it.' Both cannot be literal. Say which is meant: retention for one calendar week after the migration, or retention until closure (the safer reading, but then stop calling it a week).

findings.topic: pre-auth build-id oracle
findings.section: Shim pre-list ordering (Phase 0 / cookie package / Phase 4 front door)
findings.message: Ordering the X-Anchor-Build check BEFORE auth means any unauthenticated client can harvest the current build id from the structured 409's `expected` field. The UX rationale is sound and the leak is trivial, but a plan this rigorous about OPEN_ROUTES justifications should record the pre-auth 409 as an accepted, reviewed disclosure (one line in the OPEN_ROUTES artifact or the package), not leave it implicit.

findings.topic: Tier-2 snapshot coherence across processes
findings.section: Phase 3 — two-tier parity gate / writer model
findings.message: The Tier-2 gate 'derives views from a WRITE_LOCK-bracketed snapshot copy' — but WRITE_LOCK is an in-process lock in the DASHBOARD. Post-split, the supervisor appends to its own segment and writes its own legacy job records concurrently, outside any lock the snapshot can take. If the snapshot copies the journal segments BEFORE the legacy stores, a supervisor write landing between the two copies produces a legacy-ahead delta — which your own classification calls BUG, never-self-clearing, phase-gate-blocking. The plan never specifies snapshot ordering (legacy-first, journal-second, so the journal is always at-least-as-new) nor acknowledges that the lock cannot bracket a second process. As written, the live gate can manufacture false BUGs on a healthy post-split system, and BUG is defined as un-clearable. Specify the cross-store snapshot ordering as binding, and re-walk Scenario A/B against the two-process case.

findings.topic: legacy-ahead BUG has no repair path
findings.section: Phase 3 — emit() fail-open rule + three-class parity gate
findings.message: The fail-open rule makes emit() failure a DESIGNED-TOLERATED event ('logs loudly, counter increments, legacy write proceeds'), and the plan itself says the resulting hole 'shows up as legacy-ahead=BUG'. But BUG is defined as 'never self-clears, blocks the phase gate until root-caused' — and root-causing does not converge the stores. The replay tool only applies journal→legacy; there is no journal-backfill-from-legacy tool, and the 'no writes to journal/ outside journal.py' scan forbids ad-hoc injection. So a single transient disk hiccup during emit produces a permanent, unrepairable RED that blocks gates forever. A tolerated failure mode mapping to an unrepairable gate state is an internal contradiction. Either define a blessed backfill path inside journal.py (emitting a marked reconstruction event), or define a documented BUG-resolution procedure that actually has an edge back to GREEN.

findings.topic: replayability not uniform per event type
findings.section: Writer model / Scenario B / Phase 3 replay tool
findings.message: Scenario B asserts the replay 'idempotently re-executes the lost legacy write (the pointer-record is written)' — but doc_persisted's legacy effect is not one write; it is copy-files-from-worktree + git commit + pointer-record + index entry. The plan never specifies WHERE in that multi-step sequence emit() sits (journal-first relative to which step?), and if the crash lands before the file copy, the doc bytes exist only in a worktree the boot reaper may since have deleted — the intent is then physically unreplayable from the event, no matter how complete the payload. The payload-completeness gate proves the RECORD is reconstructible, not the EFFECT. The replay tool needs a per-type replayability column (fully-replayable / record-only / unreplayable-report-honestly), and multi-step legacy mutations need a defined emit placement. The walked scenario chose the hardest family and hand-waved exactly its hard part.

findings.topic: job-object kill-on-close vs supervisor-restart survival
findings.section: Phase 5b — live probe (b)
findings.message: Probe (b) asserts a sacrificial child SURVIVES a supervisor restart ('job-object breakaway proven'). But the existing job-object attach (proc_probe.attach_to_job_object, cited by the intake as an asset) exists precisely for owner-dies→children-die orphan prevention, i.e. kill-on-close semantics — under which probe (b) fails BY CONSTRUCTION. Making children survive supervisor restart requires breakaway or dropping KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE, which directly weakens the tree-kill cancel path and the zombie/orphan discipline the 2026-06-30 swarm-safety work depends on. The plan asserts the probe as a testable given without naming this design decision (per-job job objects without kill-on-close? explicit tree-kill for cancel + zombie-hunter for orphans?). Note C4 only requires jobs to survive DASHBOARD restart — if supervisor-restart survival is extra hardening, say so and make its job-object configuration an explicit Phase-5a contract row, not an assumed assert.

findings.topic: byte-diff gate hollow at the f-string increment
findings.section: Phase 1 — pinned-fixture dual render
findings.message: The parity gate claims 'diffed byte-for-byte' across all three increments, with an enumerated-delta list for dynamic values. But increment 3's whole point is replacing every server-side {expr} with a window.ANCHOR_BOOT read — a STRUCTURAL delta at every interpolation site. Either the gate defines a normalization step (substitute the boot JSON values into the new static output before diffing, restoring true byte equality), or the enumerated-delta list must whitelist a delta at each of the N interpolation sites — at which point the gate is weakest exactly where the risk concentrates (the census's own 'only genuinely fiddly part'). As written the mechanism is underspecified for the one increment that needs it most; increments 1–2 get a real guarantee, increment 3 gets a list of exemptions. Specify the substitution-normalized diff as the binding mechanism.

findings.topic: parity state machine missing self-clear edge
findings.section: Scenario A vs Scenario B / C3 state machine
findings.message: Scenario A's tail-window footnote says a clock-step demotion to REPAIRABLE 'self-heals on the next run' once the in-flight legacy write lands. But the binding state machine is stated as exactly 'GREEN → RED(repairable, rows named) → replay --apply → GREEN', and Scenario B's day-7 walk shows REPAIRABLE persisting until an operator acts. Both behaviors are individually sensible (a repairable row whose legacy write subsequently lands stops diverging), but the state machine as written omits the self-clear edge Scenario A relies on — the two walked scenarios contradict the machine that claims to be 'code, not decree'. Add the RED(repairable)→GREEN-without-replay edge (divergence vanished on re-derive) explicitly.

findings.topic: CLI seq allocation under the per-append lock
findings.section: Writer model — cli segment
findings.message: Two concurrent anchor.py invocations both recover writer_seq 'from the segment tail'. If the msvcrt/fcntl lock brackets only the APPEND, both read tail=N, both allocate N+1, and the serialized appends produce a duplicate (cli, N+1) — which your gate classifies BUG, never-self-clearing. The lock must bracket read-tail + allocate-seq + append as one critical section; the plan says 'per-append OS file lock', which reads as append-only. One sentence fixes it; unfixed, ordinary concurrent CLI use manufactures permanent BUGs.

findings.topic: enrollment-before-enforce intra-phase ordering
findings.section: Phase 4 — wave ordering
findings.message: The cookie/auth package (/login, /api/login, enrollment) and the GET-data-plane enforce flips both live inside Phase 4, but no intra-phase edge orders them: flipping any browser-navigated GET route to enforce before /login ships strands every browser at a 401 (the X-Anchor-Build pre-check only helps stale-BUILD clients, not unenrolled current ones). The plan is explicit about cross-deploy sequencing ('auth flips never ship in the same deploy as the JS calling them') yet silent on this larger ordering. State it as a wave-order rule: enrollment routes + login flow land and soak before the first page-route enforce flip.

findings.topic: static year-lived deterministic cookie
findings.section: Cookie/auth package
findings.message: HMAC(fixed-context, ANCHOR_TOKEN) is a DETERMINISTIC value — identical for every client, every device, for the full Max-Age 365d, revocable only by rotating the token itself (which logs out everything). Anyone who observes the cookie once (plain-HTTP localhost sniff, a shared HAR, a synced browser profile) holds a year-long GET credential to the entire data plane including /artifact, with no per-device revocation and no expiry binding. This may be an acceptable trade for a single-user Tailscale-fronted box, but the plan presents the mechanics without recording it as a considered decision; the North Star's 'cookie or equivalent' deserves one sentence of threat-model acceptance (or a cheap improvement: include a server-side epoch/nonce in the HMAC so cookies can be invalidated without token rotation).

findings.topic: drain quiescence vs multi-hour lane jobs
findings.section: Phase 0 drain script / per-wave smoke ritual
findings.message: Pre-5b, the drain script BLOCKS while a lane job runs, and every wave's merge requires drain → nssm restart. Real lane jobs (Foreman builds) run for hours and are exactly what John runs daily — so through Phases 0–5a (most of the plan) the deploy cadence is hostage to job quiescence, with the only relief an override that accepts killing the job. The plan states the check but no scheduling mitigation (deploy windows, coordinate with the parked ship-v1 build, queue deploys behind job completion). Name the operational policy now; otherwise C7's 'never-broken increments' quietly becomes 'increments whenever no job is running', discovered mid-build.

findings.topic: 5a∥4 concurrency is reordering, not parallelism
findings.section: Dependency DAG — Phase 5a concurrent with Phase 4
findings.message: Under Foreman's single-threaded wave execution, '5a runs CONCURRENT with Phase 4' cannot mean parallel wall-clock work — it means the waves may interleave. The claim 'the jobs-half now starts at the plan's midpoint' is honest as an ordering statement but the DAG's language implies schedule compression that the build topology cannot deliver (except via the warn-soak days, which are calendar waits Phase 5a waves could genuinely fill). Say 'interleavable' and note the soak-day overlap as the actual win.
